synopsis: The existing warning system alerts the operator, whereas adding automatic braking changes machine motion and moves the function across ISO 19014-2’s boundary from excluded awareness systems to motion-control safety functions [f380, f2075, f10521]. ISO 16001:2017 covers warning rather than braking, while ISO 21815 covers collision avoidance through speed reduction, stopping or motion inhibit; ISO 21815-1:2022 does not permit automatic steering [f161, f5061, f5909]. Common detection and warning-stage metrics remain comparable, but braking measures need new safety requirements, and the warning system’s field history does not transfer to the braking function [f5498, f5445, f7938]. Evidence is weighted toward warning and immature systems: the 2022 NIOSH review covered 97 cases, only 10% involving avoidance, while a seven-day 2004 radar study classified 42% of 580 alarms as nuisance alarms and 18% as false alarms [f5933, f5934, f3011]. The research found neither an off-road standard accepting simulation instead of physical collision-avoidance tests nor a documented full validation in about four months for a new machine family; synthetic-only reliability evidence and warning-data-to-braking certification precedents were also absent [f7539, f1255, f6690, f1253]. The MSHA surface-equipment rule does not mandate collision avoidance, while a multi-year Applied Intuition–Komatsu partnership announced on 9 September 2025 includes Level 9 collision avoidance for staffed operations, indicating development activity rather than closing the validation gaps [f1369, f8399, f8400, f10425].
